Arrays.question: What is an array?

options.A: A collection of elements stored in a linear structure
options.C: A method used only for sorting

Arrays.explanation: An array is a linear data structure that stores a collection of elements, typically accessed using an index.

Arrays.question: How are elements commonly accessed in an array?
Arrays.explanation: Array elements are commonly accessed using their index position.

Arrays.question: What is the index of the first element in a zero-based array?
Arrays.explanation: In zero-based indexing, the first element is stored at index 0.

Arrays.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index in a typical array?
Arrays.explanation: Direct array indexing generally provides constant-time O(1) access.

Arrays.question: What is the typical time complexity of searching an unsorted array using linear search?
Arrays.explanation: Linear search may need to inspect every element, giving O(n) time complexity.

Arrays.question: What happens when an element is inserted at the beginning of an array and existing elements must move?

options.A: Elements may need to be shifted to make space

Arrays.explanation: Inserting at the beginning can require shifting existing elements to higher indexes.

Arrays.question: What is the typical time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of an array?
Arrays.explanation: Elements may need to be shifted, so insertion at the beginning typically takes O(n) time.

Arrays.question: What is a two-dimensional array commonly used to represent?

options.A: A matrix or table of values

Arrays.explanation: A two-dimensional array organizes elements using rows and columns and can represent matrices or tables.

Arrays.question: Which operation visits every element of an array once?
Arrays.explanation: Array traversal means visiting each element, usually once, to process or inspect it.

Arrays.question: What is the main advantage of an array over a linked list for direct element access?
Arrays.explanation: Arrays support direct access by index, typically in O(1) time.

Arrays.question: What is the main disadvantage of inserting elements into the middle of an array?

options.A: Elements after the insertion position may need to be shifted
options.C: The first element is always removed

Arrays.explanation: Insertion into the middle can require shifting many subsequent elements.

Arrays.question: For a sorted array, which search algorithm can provide O(log n) search time?
Arrays.explanation: Binary search repeatedly divides the sorted search range in half, giving O(log n) time.

Arrays.question: If an array contains n elements and an algorithm compares every pair of elements, what is its typical time complexity?
Arrays.explanation: Comparing every pair of elements results in approximately n² comparisons, giving O(n²) complexity.

Linked Lists.question: What is a linked list?

options.A: A linear data structure made of nodes connected by links
options.B: A collection of sorted arrays only

Linked Lists.explanation: A linked list consists of nodes where each node stores data and one or more links to other nodes.

Linked Lists.question: What are the two common components of a singly linked list node?

options.A: Data and a link to the next node

Linked Lists.explanation: A singly linked list node normally contains data and a reference to the next node.

Linked Lists.question: What does the head of a linked list represent?

options.A: The first node of the list

Linked Lists.explanation: The head reference points to the first node in a linked list.

Linked Lists.question: What does the next pointer of the last node in a singly linked list normally contain?

options.A: A reference to the first node

Linked Lists.explanation: The last node's next pointer is normally NULL or None, indicating the end of the list.

Linked Lists.question: What is one major advantage of a linked list over a fixed-size array?

options.A: It can grow and shrink dynamically
options.B: It always provides O(1) random access

Linked Lists.explanation: Linked lists can dynamically allocate nodes as needed instead of requiring a fixed size.

Linked Lists.question: What is the typical time complexity of inserting a node at the beginning of a linked list when the head is known?
Linked Lists.explanation: The new node can be linked directly before the current head, requiring constant time.

Linked Lists.question: What is the typical time complexity of accessing the kth element of a singly linked list?
Linked Lists.explanation: A singly linked list must be traversed from the head to reach the kth node, taking O(k) time.

Linked Lists.question: What additional pointer does a doubly linked list node usually contain?
Linked Lists.explanation: A doubly linked list node usually contains both next and previous references.

Linked Lists.question: What makes a circular linked list different from a standard singly linked list?

options.A: The last node links back to a node in the list, commonly the head
options.C: It always has exactly two nodes
options.D: Every node contains two previous pointers

Linked Lists.explanation: In a circular linked list, the final node points back to the beginning or another designated node instead of NULL.

Linked Lists.question: Why is random access slower in a linked list than in an array?

options.A: Linked lists require traversal through nodes
options.D: Linked lists cannot contain more than ten nodes

Linked Lists.explanation: Linked lists do not provide direct index-based access, so nodes must usually be traversed sequentially.

Linked Lists.question: What is required to delete the first node of a singly linked list?

options.A: Move the head to the second node
options.C: Move the tail to the first node

Linked Lists.explanation: Deleting the first node is done by updating head to point to the second node.

Linked Lists.question: If a linked list contains n nodes, what is the typical time complexity of searching for a value in an unsorted list?
Linked Lists.explanation: An unsorted linked list may require checking every node, resulting in O(n) search time.

Linked Lists.question: Which technique can be used to detect a cycle in a linked list using O(1) extra space?

options.A: Floyd's slow and fast pointer algorithm

Linked Lists.explanation: Floyd's cycle detection algorithm uses slow and fast pointers to detect whether a linked list contains a cycle.

Stacks.question: What principle does a stack follow?
Stacks.explanation: A stack follows Last In, First Out (LIFO), meaning the most recently inserted item is removed first.

Stacks.question: What is the operation of adding an element to a stack called?
Stacks.explanation: Push adds an element to the top of a stack.

Stacks.question: What is the operation of removing the top element from a stack called?
Stacks.explanation: Pop removes and returns the top element of a stack.

Stacks.question: What does the peek operation do on a stack?

options.B: Returns the top element without removing it
options.C: Adds an element to the bottom

Stacks.explanation: Peek examines the top element without removing it.

Stacks.question: What is stack underflow?

options.A: Trying to pop from an empty stack
options.B: Adding too many elements to a queue

Stacks.explanation: Stack underflow occurs when an operation attempts to remove an element from an empty stack.

Stacks.question: What is stack overflow in a fixed-capacity stack?

options.A: Attempting to push an element when the stack is full
options.B: Attempting to pop an empty stack

Stacks.explanation: Stack overflow occurs when an insertion is attempted on a full fixed-capacity stack.

Stacks.question: What is the typical time complexity of push and pop operations in a well-implemented stack?
Stacks.explanation: Push and pop operate at the top of the stack and can normally be performed in O(1) time.

Stacks.question: Which application commonly uses a stack?
Stacks.explanation: The call stack manages active function calls and their execution contexts.

Stacks.question: Which data structure is commonly used to implement undo operations?
Stacks.explanation: Undo operations commonly use a stack because the most recent action is undone first.

Stacks.question: Which algorithm commonly uses a stack to evaluate postfix expressions?
Stacks.explanation: A stack is used to store operands while evaluating postfix expressions.

Stacks.question: How can a stack be used to check balanced parentheses?

options.A: Push opening brackets and pop when matching closing brackets appear
options.D: Use binary search on the brackets

Stacks.explanation: Opening brackets are pushed onto the stack and matching closing brackets remove them.

Stacks.question: Which traversal of a binary tree can naturally be implemented using a stack?
Stacks.explanation: Depth-first traversals can be implemented iteratively using a stack.

Stacks.question: Why does recursion naturally use a stack?

options.A: Each recursive call needs a stack frame to store its execution state
options.D: Each recursive call creates a database

Stacks.explanation: Function calls are stored as stack frames, and recursive calls build additional frames until they return.

Queues.question: What principle does a queue follow?
Queues.explanation: A queue follows First In, First Out (FIFO), meaning the earliest inserted element is removed first.

Queues.question: What operation adds an element to a queue?
Queues.explanation: Enqueue adds an element to the rear of a queue.

Queues.question: What operation removes an element from a queue?
Queues.explanation: Dequeue removes an element from the front of a queue.

Queues.question: From which end is an element normally removed in a standard queue?
Queues.explanation: Elements are normally removed from the front of a queue.

Queues.question: From which end is a new element normally inserted in a standard queue?
Queues.explanation: New elements are normally inserted at the rear of a queue.

Queues.question: What is queue underflow?

options.A: Removing an element from an empty queue
options.B: Adding an element to an empty queue

Queues.explanation: Queue underflow occurs when a dequeue operation is attempted on an empty queue.

Queues.question: Which data structure is commonly used for breadth-first search?
Queues.explanation: Breadth-first search uses a queue to process vertices level by level.

Queues.question: What is a circular queue?

options.A: A queue where the end can wrap around to the beginning
options.B: A queue that contains only one element

Queues.explanation: A circular queue treats the storage as connected in a circle so freed positions can be reused.

Queues.question: What is the main advantage of a circular queue over a simple array-based queue?

options.A: It can reuse positions freed at the front
options.C: It removes the need for a rear

Queues.explanation: Circular queues reuse available positions by wrapping the rear around to the beginning.

Queues.question: What is a priority queue?

options.A: A queue where elements are removed according to priority
options.B: A queue that always follows insertion order

Queues.explanation: A priority queue removes elements based on their priority rather than simply their arrival order.

Queues.question: Which data structure is commonly used to implement an efficient priority queue?
Queues.explanation: Binary heaps are commonly used to implement efficient priority queues.

Queues.question: What is a deque?

options.A: A double-ended queue that allows insertion and deletion at both ends
options.B: A queue that allows insertion only at the front

Queues.explanation: A deque, or double-ended queue, supports operations at both the front and rear.

Queues.question: What is the typical time complexity of enqueue and dequeue in a properly implemented linked-list queue?
Queues.explanation: With references to both front and rear, enqueue and dequeue can be performed in constant time.

Trees.question: What is a tree in data structures?

options.A: A hierarchical non-linear data structure made of nodes
options.B: A linear structure containing only arrays

Trees.explanation: A tree is a non-linear hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges.

Trees.question: What is the topmost node of a tree called?
Trees.explanation: The root is the topmost node of a tree.

Trees.question: What is a node with no children called?
Trees.explanation: A leaf node has no children.

Trees.question: What is the relationship between a parent and its directly connected lower node?

options.A: The lower node is a child
options.B: The lower node is always the root
options.C: The lower node is a sibling
options.D: The lower node is an ancestor only

Trees.explanation: A node directly connected below another node is called its child.

Trees.question: What is a binary tree?

options.A: A tree in which each node has at most two children
options.B: A tree containing exactly two nodes
options.C: A tree containing only two levels

Trees.explanation: A binary tree is a tree where each node has at most two children.

Trees.question: What are the two possible child positions in a binary tree?
Trees.explanation: Each binary tree node can have a left child and a right child.

Trees.question: What property makes a binary search tree useful for searching?

options.A: Values in the left subtree are ordered relative to the node and values in the right subtree are ordered oppositely
options.B: Every node must have exactly two children

Trees.explanation: In a binary search tree, values in the left subtree are less than the node and values in the right subtree are greater, subject to the chosen duplicate policy.

Trees.question: Which traversal visits nodes in the order Root, Left, Right?
Trees.explanation: Preorder traversal visits the root first, followed by the left subtree and right subtree.

Trees.question: Which traversal visits nodes in the order Left, Root, Right?
Trees.explanation: Inorder traversal visits the left subtree, root, and then right subtree.

Trees.question: Which traversal visits nodes in the order Left, Right, Root?
Trees.explanation: Postorder traversal visits the left subtree, right subtree, and then the root.

Trees.question: What is the height of a tree related to?

options.A: The longest path from the root to a leaf under the chosen height convention
options.B: The total number of leaf nodes only

Trees.explanation: Tree height measures the longest root-to-leaf path, with exact counting depending on the convention used.

Trees.question: What is a balanced binary search tree designed to maintain?

options.A: A relatively small height to keep operations efficient

Trees.explanation: Balanced search trees keep their height controlled so searching, insertion, and deletion remain efficient.

Trees.question: What is the typical search time in a balanced binary search tree containing n nodes?
Trees.explanation: A balanced binary search tree has logarithmic height, giving O(log n) search time.

Graphs.question: What is a graph in data structures?

options.A: A collection of vertices connected by edges
options.B: A linear array of numbers only

Graphs.explanation: A graph consists of vertices, also called nodes, and edges that connect pairs of vertices.

Graphs.question: What are the two basic components of a graph?
Graphs.explanation: Graphs are composed of vertices and edges.

Graphs.question: What is a vertex in a graph?

options.A: A node representing an entity or point

Graphs.explanation: A vertex is a node in a graph that represents an entity or point.

Graphs.question: What is an edge in a graph?
Graphs.explanation: An edge represents a connection or relationship between vertices.

Graphs.question: What is a directed graph?

options.A: A graph whose edges have a specified direction
options.C: A graph with only one vertex
options.D: A graph that must be a tree

Graphs.explanation: In a directed graph, each edge has a direction from one vertex to another.

Graphs.question: What is an undirected graph?

options.A: A graph whose edges do not have a direction
options.D: A graph that must contain cycles

Graphs.explanation: In an undirected graph, an edge represents a connection without a specified direction.

Graphs.question: What is the degree of a vertex in an undirected graph?

options.A: The number of edges incident to the vertex
options.C: The number of roots in the graph

Graphs.explanation: The degree of a vertex in an undirected graph is the number of edges connected to it.

Graphs.question: Which traversal explores a graph level by level?
Graphs.explanation: Breadth-first search explores vertices level by level using a queue.

Graphs.question: Which data structure is commonly used by breadth-first search?
Graphs.explanation: BFS uses a queue to process vertices in breadth-first order.

Graphs.question: Which data structure is commonly used to implement depth-first search iteratively?
Graphs.explanation: An explicit stack can be used to implement iterative depth-first search.

Graphs.question: What is an adjacency matrix?

options.A: A two-dimensional representation showing relationships between pairs of vertices
options.B: A linked list containing only roots

Graphs.explanation: An adjacency matrix uses a two-dimensional array to represent whether pairs of vertices are connected, often storing edge weights when applicable.

Graphs.question: What is an adjacency list?

options.A: A representation that stores a list of neighboring vertices for each vertex
options.B: A table containing only graph names
options.D: A queue containing all edges in sorted order

Graphs.explanation: An adjacency list stores the neighbors of each vertex and is often memory-efficient for sparse graphs.

Graphs.question: Which algorithm is commonly used to find shortest paths from a source in a graph with non-negative edge weights?
Graphs.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source vertex when edge weights are non-negative.
